claim: In the United Kingdom, 81.4% of white students and 68.0% of Black, Asian, and other minority ethnic (BAME) students are awarded good undergraduate degrees (first or upper second), which equates to an award gap of 13.4%.
source: In the United Kingdom (UK), 81.4% of white students and 68.0% of Black, Asian, and other minority ethnic (BAME) students are awarded good undergraduate degrees (where good means a first or upper second), which equates to an award gap of 13.4% (see Methods for more details on the use of the term BAME in this article).
evidence: The claim cites specific percentages and defines the award gap calculation, representing quantitative data about UK undergraduate degree outcomes.

claim: The existence of an award gap has been known about for over 25 years.
source: The existence of an award gap has been known about for over 25 years, and such gaps have been reported for every university in the UK (AdvanceHE, 2020b; Woolf et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published reports documenting the historical awareness of the award gap.

claim: Award gaps have been reported for every university in the UK.
source: The existence of an award gap has been known about for over 25 years, and such gaps have been reported for every university in the UK (AdvanceHE, 2020b; Woolf et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published reports documenting award gaps across UK universities.

claim: Similar gaps have been reported in the Netherlands, United States (US) and Australia for undergraduate and postgraduate taught degrees, and other college-level courses.
source: Similar gaps have also been reported in the Netherlands, United States (US) and Australia for undergraduate and postgraduate taught degrees, and other college-level courses (Stegers-Jager et al., 2016; Kleshinski et al., 2009; Tekian et al., 2001; Alexander et al., 2009; Harris et al., 2020; Haak et al., 2011; Rath et al., 2012; Farmer, 2017; Kay-Lambkin et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies from different countries documenting similar award gaps.

claim: Studies in the US, UK and the Netherlands have reported gaps in the marks awarded to different ethnic groups for various qualifying exams for both undergraduate and postgraduate courses.
source: Indeed, studies in the US, UK and the Netherlands have reported gaps in the marks awarded to different ethnic groups for various qualifying exams for both undergraduate and postgraduate courses (Miller and Stassun, 2014; Miller et al., 2019; Reeves and Halikias, 2017; Stegers-Jager et al., 2016; UK Government, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting gaps in entrance exam scores.

claim: The award gap between ethnic groups persists when comparing students entering higher education with the same qualifications in both the UK and the US.
source: However, when tested directly in both the UK and the US, the award gap between ethnic groups persists when comparing students entering higher education with the same qualifications (Amos and Doku, 2019; Tekian et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that controlled for entrance qualifications.

claim: Despite students from Chinese and Indian ethnic backgrounds outperforming white students in university entrance exams in the UK, an award gap of 5% still exists for both of these minority groups.
source: Furthermore, despite students from Chinese and Indian ethnic backgrounds outperforming white students in university entrance exams in the UK, an award gap of 5% still exists for both of these minority groups (UK Government, 2020; AdvanceHE, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to government and higher education reports documenting entrance exam performance and award gaps.

claim: Institutions themselves are responsible for the award gap between white and BAME students.
source: These analyses indicate that institutions themselves are responsible for the award gap between white and BAME students.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the preceding analysis showing that entrance qualifications do not explain the gap.

claim: Racism or unconscious (implicit) bias is unlikely to be a major cause of the award gap since most marking is blind.
source: Within the context of marking students' work, racism or unconscious (implicit) bias is unlikely since most marking is blind, and when it is not (such as in clinical work) it has been found to be an unlikely major cause (McManus et al., 2013; Woolf et al., 2011; Yeates et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining bias in marking and by the fact that marking is typically blind.

claim: Studies investigating the cause of the award gap have controlled for over 20 other potential factors, such as poverty, age, prior school type and learning style, yet a large, unexplained award gap still remains.
source: Other studies investigating the cause of the award gap have controlled for over 20 other potential factors, such as poverty, age, prior school type and learning style. Yet, while some of these factors have been found to make a contribution, a large, unexplained award gap still remains (Broeke and Nicholls, 2007; Woolf et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that controlled for multiple factors but still found an unexplained gap.

claim: The proportion of white graduates in employment or further education one year after graduation is a third higher than the proportion of BAME graduates.
source: The award gap follows BAME students into their careers: the proportion of white graduates in employment or further education one year after graduation is a third higher than the proportion of BAME graduates (UK Government, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to UK Government data on graduate employment outcomes.

claim: Only 9.1% of professors are BAME, compared with 14% of the population in England and Wales, and 40% in London.
source: Moreover, only 9.1% of professors are BAME (AdvanceHE, 2020a), compared with 14% of the population in England and Wales, and 40% in London (White, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reports documenting the proportion of BAME professors and population demographics.

claim: Most of the attrition of BAME students takes place at the transition from undergraduate to PhD student, and the transition from PhD student to postdoctoral researcher.
source: Most of this attrition takes place at the transition from undergraduate to PhD student, and the transition from PhD student to postdoctoral researcher (see Methods for the trajectory; AdvanceHE, 2020a; AdvanceHE, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reports documenting career progression data.

claim: Selection for interview for the most competitive and prestigious PhD positions tend to go to those students with the highest grade (first or high upper second), which fewer BAME students possess.
source: In practice, selection for interview for the most competitive and prestigious PhD positions – which appear to increase the chances of progressing further in an academic research career – tend to go to those students with the highest grade (that is, to students with a first, or students with an upper second overall with a first or high upper second in the relevant modules), which fewer BAME students possess (AdvanceHE, 2020b; this report).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a report and data from the current study showing fewer BAME students achieve top grades.

claim: Black Caribbean PhD students are less likely than other PhD students to have a fully-funded UK Research Council Studentship.
source: There is little direct data, but this notion is consistent with the observation that Black Caribbean PhD students are less likely than other PhD students to have a fully-funded UK Research Council Studentship (a pre-doctoral fellowship that is considered to be highly competitive; Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting funding disparities for Black Caribbean PhD students.

claim: Other inequalities linked to the undergraduate degree, such as disparities in information on application processes and prior university attended, also likely contribute to reducing the chance of a BAME student progressing to PhD.
source: It is important to note, however, that other inequalities linked to the undergraduate degree, such as disparities in information on application processes and prior university attended, also likely contribute to reducing the chance of a BAME student progressing to PhD (Williams et al., 2019) or receiving an interview for doctorate positions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study and represents speculation about contributing factors.

claim: Considerably fewer school leavers (of all white and minority ethnic groups combined) who live in the most deprived neighbourhoods progress to higher education.
source: Furthermore, previous data have shown that other inequalities also contribute to career outcomes in the UK: for example, considerably fewer school leavers (of all white and minority ethnic groups combined) who live in the most deprived neighbourhoods progress to higher education (Sosu and Ellis, 2014; UCAS, 2019), and Pakistani, Black, or Roma/Gypsy/Irish/other traveller ethnic groups are awarded fewer high grades in end-of-school exams (UK Government, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting socioeconomic disparities in higher education access.

claim: Pakistani, Black, or Roma/Gypsy/Irish/other traveller ethnic groups are awarded fewer high grades in end-of-school exams.
source: Furthermore, previous data have shown that other inequalities also contribute to career outcomes in the UK: for example, considerably fewer school leavers (of all white and minority ethnic groups combined) who live in the most deprived neighbourhoods progress to higher education (Sosu and Ellis, 2014; UCAS, 2019), and Pakistani, Black, or Roma/Gypsy/Irish/other traveller ethnic groups are awarded fewer high grades in end-of-school exams (UK Government, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to UK Government data on end-of-school exam performance.

claim: In the US, the ethnicity award gap (and to a lesser extent, gender gaps) in the graduate record exams (GRE) leads to higher rejection rates for these minority groups when applying to PhD positions, or even prevents them from applying.
source: A similar effect is also seen in the US, where the ethnicity award gap (and to a lesser extent, gender gaps) in the graduate record exams (GRE) leads to higher rejection rates for these minority groups when applying to PhD positions, or even prevents them from applying (Hodapp and Woodle, 2017; Miller and Stassun, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting the impact of GRE gaps on PhD applications.

claim: The transitions to PhD and postdoc positions show by far the largest loss of talent of minority ethnic groups.
source: However, the transitions to PhD and postdoc positions show by far the largest loss of talent of minority ethnic groups, so focusing resources on these transitions is likely to have the largest impact.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the previously cited data on attrition at these career stages.

claim: The award gap can vary from subject to subject – from 3% to 22% in the UK.
source: Furthermore, the fact the gap can vary from subject to subject – from 3% to 22% in the UK (AdvanceHE, 2020b) – is often not considered.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a report documenting variation in award gaps across subjects.

claim: Different solutions (or different combinations of solutions) may be needed for different subjects to address the award gap.
source: This suggests that different solutions (or different combinations of solutions) may be needed for different subjects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that award gaps vary by subject.

claim: 47.0% (372/792) of the cell biology students assigned themselves as having BAME ethnicity.
source: 47.0% (372/792) of the cell biology students assigned themselves as having BAME ethnicity, and 63.3% (501/792) were UK-domiciled.
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from the study cohort.

claim: 63.3% (501/792) of the cell biology students were UK-domiciled.
source: 47.0% (372/792) of the cell biology students assigned themselves as having BAME ethnicity, and 63.3% (501/792) were UK-domiciled.
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from the study cohort.

claim: At UCL, the award gap for UK students is 4.9% on average based on the marks of 8,044 undergraduate students that started their graduation year between 2016–2018.
source: At UCL, the gap for its UK students is 4.9% on average based on the marks of 8,044 undergraduate students that started their graduation year between 2016–2018, which are similar cohort years to those in this study (Table 1).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from UCL student records.

claim: The UCL award gap for UK students (4.9%) is at the smaller end of the scale compared to the average gap for all UK students (13.4%).
source: This is at the smaller end of the scale compared to the average gap for all UK students (13.4%).
evidence: The claim compares UCL data to national data, representing a comparative analysis.

claim: The average gap between BAME and white international undergraduate students at UCL (N = 5,671 total) is 6.3%.
source: In these same UCL cohorts, the average gap between BAME and white international undergraduate students (N = 5,671 total) is 6.3%, which is near the 4.9% for UK students.
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from UCL student records.

claim: If any domicile effect exists on the award gap, it is small.
source: This suggests that if any domicile effect exists, it is small.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of award gaps between UK and international students.

claim: The mean admission tariff for BAME (50.53 ± 0.15) and white (50.29 ± 0.33) students included in this study were virtually identical.
source: The mean admission tariff for BAME (50.53 ± 0.15) and white (50.29 ± 0.33) students included in this study were virtually identical (Figure 1A): the equivalent of nearly all students in each of these ethnic groupings gaining one A* grade and two A grades (which would be a mean tariff of 50.7).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from A-level entrance qualifications and references Figure 1A.

claim: The mean entrance tariff for cell biology students is very similar to the mean entrance tariff for all BAME (50.27 ± 0.06) and all white (50.03 ± 0.01) undergraduate students who entered UCL with A-levels for the same cohort years.
source: These data are very similar to the mean entrance tariff for all BAME (50.27 ± 0.06) and all white (50.03 ± 0.01) undergraduate students who entered UCL with A-levels for the same cohort years as these cell biology students (2013, 2014, 2015 entrants).
evidence: The claim compares cell biology student data to broader UCL data, representing a comparative analysis.

claim: Of the total grades awarded to BAME students, 95.45% ± 1.01 were A* or A, and for white students this figure was 95.02% ± 0.62.
source: As expected distributions for BAME and white students were nearly identical (Figure 1B); of the total grades awarded to BAME students 95.45% ± 1.01 were A* or A, and for white students this figure was 95.02% ± 0.62 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from A-level entrance qualifications and references Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Proportionally fewer BAME students were awarded good grades for cell biology in year 2 compared to their admission qualifications.
source: Looking at the grades awarded to the same three cohorts of students in year 2 of their biosciences, natural sciences or other degree revealed that proportionally fewer of these same BAME students were awarded good grades for cell biology (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing admission grades to year 2 cell biology grades and references Figure 1C.

claim: The mean of all marks awarded in year 2 cell biology was a low 2i (60–64%) for BAME students and a high 2i (65–69%) for white students.
source: The mean of all marks awarded was a low 2i (60–64%) for BAME students and a high 2i (65–69%) for white students (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from year 2 cell biology marks and references Figure 1C.

claim: Prior qualifications do not explain the subsequent award gap in cell biology, at least at the resolution that the A-level grading system permits.
source: These data indicate that prior qualifications do not explain the subsequent award gap in cell biology, at least at the resolution that the A-level grading system permits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of similar A-level grades but different cell biology outcomes.

claim: The finding that prior qualifications do not explain the award gap is in line with other admission studies at UK universities.
source: This is in line with other admission studies at UK universities (Amos and Doku, 2019; Broeke and Nicholls, 2007; Woolf et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to other studies with similar findings.

claim: In all year 1, year 2 and year 3 courses in the study, proportionally fewer BAME students were awarded final good grades than white students.
source: In all year 1, year 2 and year 3 courses in the study, proportionally fewer BAME students were awarded final good grades than white students (Figure 2A, B and E).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from cell biology courses and references Figure 2A, B and E.

claim: The award gap has appeared by year 1 at the University of Nottingham.
source: That the award gap has appeared by year 1 has also been reported for the University of Nottingham (Amos and Doku, 2019) and is the case for all undergraduate degrees at UCL (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study at another university and data from UCL.

claim: The average gap in good grades awarded each year of study in cell biology (~8–13%) and across UCL (~7–11%) were similar.
source: The average gap in good grades awarded each year of study in cell biology (~8–13%) and across UCL (~7–11%) were similar (Figure 2, compare E and F, final mark).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing cell biology gaps to UCL-wide gaps and references Figure 2E and F.

claim: The gaps identified in cell biology are in the range expected for students studying at UCL.
source: This suggests that the gaps identified in cell biology are in the range expected for students studying at UCL.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of cell biology gaps to UCL-wide gaps.

claim: For 11 out of 12 sets of marks studied, the award gap seemed largely derived from the exam component of the course.
source: For 11 out of 12 sets of marks studied, this award gap seemed largely derived from the exam component of the course (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from the analysis of course components and references Figure 2C-E.

claim: The average exam gaps were similar in year 1 and 2 at over 13% each, and most pronounced in year 3 at nearly 17%.
source: The average exam gaps were similar in year 1 and 2 at over 13% each, and most pronounced in year 3 at nearly 17% (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from exam component analysis and references Figure 2E.

claim: No exam gap was detected in year 2, cohort 4.
source: No exam gap was detected in year 2, cohort 4 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from exam component analysis and references Figure 2C.

claim: In year 2, cohort 4, a gap overall was still observed due to a longer 'tail' of lower exam marks for BAME students which resulted in fewer BAME students (61.3%; 23/36) being able to use their coursework grade to obtain a good final mark compared to white students (88.5%; 23/26).
source: However, a gap overall was still observed for this group (Figure 2A). This was explained by a longer 'tail' of lower exam marks for BAME students which resulted in fewer BAME students (61.3%; 23/36) being able to use their coursework grade to obtain a good final mark compared to white students (88.5%; 23/26).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data explaining the overall gap despite no exam gap and references Figure 2A.

claim: The coursework award gap in good grades was smaller than the exam gap in all individual cohorts and cell biology courses in year 1 (4/4) and year 3 (4/4); and most of the cohorts in year 2 (3/4).
source: The coursework award gap in good grades was smaller than the exam gap in all individual cohorts and cell biology courses in year 1 (4/4) and year 3 (4/4); and most of the cohorts in year 2 (3/4) (Figure 2C,D, compare solid and dashed lines).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing exam and coursework gaps and references Figure 2C and D.

claim: The coursework award gap was 7.1- (year 1), 13.1- (year 2) and 3.1- (year 3) times smaller than the exam award gap on average.
source: The coursework award gap was 7.1- (year 1), 13.1- (year 2) and 3.1- (year 3) times smaller than the exam award gap on average (Figure 2E, compare exam and coursework values).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing exam and coursework gaps and references Figure 2E.

claim: The pattern of smaller coursework gaps compared to exam gaps is reproducible and therefore significant.
source: Taken together this suggests a reproducible and therefore significant pattern.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the consistent pattern observed across multiple cohorts and years.

claim: The small coursework award gap (1–2%) for the year 1–2 pathway reflects small fluctuations in different admission years.
source: It is speculated that the small coursework award gap (1–2%) for the year 1–2 pathway in this study reflects small fluctuations in different admission years: this is consistent with 5/8 incidences where BAME students were awarded equal, near equal or slightly higher proportion of good marks for the coursework than white students (observable in Figure 2C, compare dashed lines).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observed patterns in the data and references Figure 2C.

claim: The coursework effect in year 3 courses (average 5% award gap) is consistently small.
source: In contrast, although different admission years cannot be evaluated in the year three study as they were necessarily aggregated (see An exploration of the award gap in cell biology courses), there is no such fluctuation, suggesting that the coursework effect in year 3 courses in this study (average 5% award gap) is consistently small (Figure 2D, compare dashed lines).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of fluctuation in year 3 data and references Figure 2D.

claim: When the grades awarded for the exam and coursework were similarly high, a relatively large award gap between white and BAME students was still distinguishable for the exam, but was small or none for the coursework of the same cohort.
source: However, when the grades awarded for the exam and coursework were similarly high as each other (such as cohorts 1 and 3 in year 1 for white students) a relatively large award gap between white and BAME students was still distinguishable for the exam, but was small or none for the coursework of the same cohort (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing exam and coursework gaps when overall performance is high and references Figure 2C.

claim: It is unlikely that larger gaps are only revealed when tasks are harder.
source: Similarly, it is unlikely that larger gaps are only revealed when tasks are harder: for example, in year 3, which is expected to have harder coursework tasks overall, grades were broadly the same for exams and coursework (for white students), yet the gap in grades awarded to BAME and white students were only evident in the exam.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that exam gaps persist even when coursework is expected to be harder.

claim: Cohen's D revealed that the effect for coursework is three to six times smaller than the exam.
source: Cohen's D (which is a measure of effect size) was then applied to the mean award gap of all four cohorts or courses studied for each component in the year 1–2 pathway and year 3 study. This revealed that the effect for coursework is three to six times smaller than the exam (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from statistical analysis and references Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In year 2 and year 3 cell biology, a larger coursework gap could not be found when comparing every absolute mark awarded to BAME and white students at the resolution of 5% intervals from less than 30% to 100% scores.
source: However, in year 2 and year 3 cell biology a larger coursework gap could not be found when comparing every absolute mark awarded to BAME and white students at the resolution of 5% intervals (which is one-half grade band) from less than 30% to 100% scores (Figure 3; only cohorts 1–3 were included in the analysis for year 2 – see legend for more details)
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from detailed mark distribution analysis and references Figure 3.

claim: The peak of final marks and the peak of exam marks awarded to BAME students were shifted half to more than one grade band lower than white students.
source: Clearly evident in these frequency distributions, the peak of final marks (Figure 3A and B) and the peak of exam marks (Figure 3C and D) awarded to BAME students were shifted half to more than one grade band lower than white students (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from mark distribution analysis and references Figure 3A-D.

claim: BAME students are most likely to receive a low 2i (60–64%), whilst white students are more likely to receive a high 2i (65–69%) or a low first (70–74%) for these courses overall.
source: The end result is that BAME students are most likely to receive a low 2i (60–64%), whilst white students are more likely to receive a high 2i (65–69%) or a low first (70–74%) for these courses overall (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from mark distribution analysis and references Figure 3A and B.

claim: The histograms of coursework marks for white and BAME students were almost completely superimposed in both year 2 and year 3 studies.
source: In contrast, the histograms of coursework marks for white and BAME students were almost completely superimposed in both studies (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from mark distribution analysis and references Figure 3E and F.

claim: There is no larger visible gap anywhere in the entire spectrum of marks at the resolution of 5% intervals for either year 2 or 3 cell biology coursework.
source: However, clearly there is no larger visible gap anywhere in the entire spectrum of marks at the resolution of 5% intervals for either year 2 or 3 cell biology coursework (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from mark distribution analysis and references Figure 3E and F.

claim: The average award gaps for year 2 and year 3 coursework at the level of first class marks-only remained small (2.60% and 4.11%, respectively) similar to that reported at the level of all good marks for these modules (2.14% and 5.45%).
source: As expected from these histograms (Figure 3) the average award gaps for year 2 and year 3 coursework at the level of first class marks-only remained small (2.60% and 4.11%, respectively) similar to that reported at the level of all good marks for these modules (2.14% and 5.45%; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, compare A and B).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing first class and all good marks gaps and references Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average exam award gaps for first class marks in year 2 and 3 (5.60% and 9.29%) were smaller than those for good marks (18.37% and 16.75%), but importantly were two (or more) times larger than the coursework gaps at the same level.
source: The average exam award gaps for first class marks in year 2 and 3 (5.60% and 9.29%) were smaller than those for good marks (18.37% and 16.75%), but importantly were two (or more) times larger than the coursework gaps at the same level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, compare A and B).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data comparing exam and coursework gaps at first class level and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pattern of the exam award gap in first class marks being larger than the coursework award gap was observed in three out of four of the year 3 courses (B, C and D).
source: This pattern of the exam award gap in first class marks being larger than the coursework award gap was also observed in three out of four of the year 3 courses (B, C and D); in course A, both the exam and coursework award gap were similarly small (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data from individual course analysis and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In these cell biology courses, the exam is the main contributor to the gap in marks awarded for the course overall.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that in these cell biology courses, the exam is the main contributor to the gap in marks awarded for the course overall.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of exam and coursework gaps across multiple cohorts and years.

claim: If there is a contribution from coursework to the award gap, it is relatively small in all years and may not be consistently present in years 1 and 2.
source: If there is a contribution from coursework, it is relatively small in all years and may not be consistently present in years 1 and 2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis showing small and variable coursework gaps.

claim: The finding that exams produce a bigger gap than coursework is consistent with medicine where different types of assessments produce gaps of different sizes.
source: The finding is consistent with medicine where different types of assessments produce gaps of different sizes; although, unlike here, exams versus coursework were not explicitly tested (Woolf et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study in medicine showing variable gaps by assessment type.

claim: For the past 10 years, only 0.5% per year has been shaved off the undergraduate degree award gap.
source: For the past 10 years, only 0.5% per year has been shaved off the undergraduate degree award gap (AdvanceHE, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a report documenting the slow rate of gap closure.

claim: In the past 10 years there have been extensive reviews and reports that have detailed why the unexplained, award gap exists and hundreds of recommendations on how universities can tackle it.
source: Yet in the same period there have been extensive reviews and reports that have detailed why the unexplained, award gap exists and hundreds of recommendations on how universities can tackle it (Alexander and Arday, 2015; Amos and Doku, 2019; Berry and Loke, 2011; ECU and HEA, 2008; Miller, 2016; NUS, 2011; summarised in Figure 4; for a review of earlier studies (from pre-1990s) see Singh, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple reports and references Figure 4.

claim: Lack of staff time coupled to insufficient funding and resources to implement existing recommendations is reducing the speed at which the award gap is closing.
source: A scrutiny of the literature suggests that various factors are reducing the speed at which the award gap is closing: lack of staff time coupled to insufficient funding and resources to implement existing recommendations (see Policy 1); limited scientific approaches and diverse types of evidence on the underlying causes (Policy 2); limited funding for fundamental scientific studies and for applied scientific approaches on what works (Policies 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the author's analysis of the literature.

claim: Limited scientific approaches and diverse types of evidence on the underlying causes is reducing the speed at which the award gap is closing.
source: A scrutiny of the literature suggests that various factors are reducing the speed at which the award gap is closing: lack of staff time coupled to insufficient funding and resources to implement existing recommendations (see Policy 1); limited scientific approaches and diverse types of evidence on the underlying causes (Policy 2); limited funding for fundamental scientific studies and for applied scientific approaches on what works (Policies 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the author's analysis of the literature.

claim: Limited funding for fundamental scientific studies and for applied scientific approaches on what works is reducing the speed at which the award gap is closing.
source: A scrutiny of the literature suggests that various factors are reducing the speed at which the award gap is closing: lack of staff time coupled to insufficient funding and resources to implement existing recommendations (see Policy 1); limited scientific approaches and diverse types of evidence on the underlying causes (Policy 2); limited funding for fundamental scientific studies and for applied scientific approaches on what works (Policies 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the author's analysis of the literature.

claim: Many universities, including UCL, have put considerable effort into identifying what resources are needed to close the award gap, with nearly 200 recommendations in three reports alone.
source: Many universities, including UCL, have put considerable effort into identifying what resources are needed to close the award gap, with nearly 200 recommendations in three reports alone (Figure 4; Box 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4 and Box 1 summarizing recommendations.

claim: The recommendations for closing the award gap are all hugely time-intensive to develop and implement, both for academic and other university staff, and cost-heavy for universities.
source: But therein lay two fundamental issues: they are all hugely time-intensive to develop and implement, both for academic and other university staff, and cost-heavy for universities.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nature and scope of the recommendations.

claim: Academics already work excessive hours just to get their 'regular' job done.
source: Academics already work excessive hours just to get their 'regular' job done (Richardson, 2019; UCU, 2016), yet seem directly responsible for delivering many of the recommendations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reports documenting academic workload.

claim: The UK does not appear in the world's top 100 for staff-student ratios.
source: The UK does not appear in the world's top 100 for staff-student ratios (THE, 2020) and the best UK ones are misleading, as they do not measure proportion of time spent on teaching or with students.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a ranking report.

claim: Some universities (including University of the Arts London (UAL) and University of Brighton) have responded by releasing university access and other funds to hire new, permanent staff to work on the award gap.
source: Some universities (including University of the Arts London (UAL) and University of Brighton) have responded by releasing university access and other funds to hire new, permanent staff to work on the award gap, whilst others (including UCL) are enabling temporary 'buy-out' of existing staff time to develop and implement initiatives.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of specific university initiatives.

claim: At a single large university alone there are >4,400 courses (modules) within >440 separate undergraduate degrees.
source: This is welcome news; however, the total amounts to a handful of full-time equivalent posts, whereas at a single large university alone there are >4,400 courses (modules) within >440 separate undergraduate degrees (estimate based on the UCL record) and scaling that up to >50,000 undergraduate degrees across the UK (http://www.ucas.com) approaches half a million courses.
evidence: The claim is based on data from UCL records.

claim: Scaling up to >50,000 undergraduate degrees across the UK approaches half a million courses.
source: This is welcome news; however, the total amounts to a handful of full-time equivalent posts, whereas at a single large university alone there are >4,400 courses (modules) within >440 separate undergraduate degrees (estimate based on the UCL record) and scaling that up to >50,000 undergraduate degrees across the UK (http://www.ucas.com) approaches half a million courses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from scaling UCL data to the national level.

claim: The UK government provides £8 per BAME student for training and other resources to reduce the gap.
source: These positions could be made permanent which would substantially increase the £8 per BAME student provided for training and other resources to reduce the gap (see Policy 3).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation of government funding per student (detailed in Methods).

claim: Only a very small number (estimated 0.51%) of the recommendations on how to close the unexplained award gap appear to be supported by raw numerical data.
source: However, only a very small number (estimated 0.51%) of these recommendations appear to be supported by raw numerical data.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of the evidence base for recommendations.

claim: The majority of recommendations (estimate 20.3%) appear to be based on qualitative data, such as surveys, interviews and discussions.
source: The majority of these recommendations appear to be based on qualitative data (estimate 20.3%), such as surveys, interviews and discussions, particularly those related to the following two categories which represent nearly one-quarter of all the recommendations: student experience of university life and sense of belonging; teaching and learning practice and the degree curriculum (Figure 4; see also Methods for other details).
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of the evidence base for recommendations and references Figure 4.

claim: A recent comprehensive analysis of what 99 UK higher education institutions are currently doing concluded that 'a far more scientific approach' is one of the top five most outstanding actions required to close the award gap.
source: A recent comprehensive analysis of what 99 UK higher education institutions are currently doing concluded that 'a far more scientific approach' is one of the top five most outstanding actions required to close the award gap (Amos and Doku, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a comprehensive analysis report.

claim: Many (25/30) of the surveys and discussions to date do not seem to report control data.
source: Yet many (25/30) of the surveys and discussions to date do not seem to report control data (NUS, 2011; Methods).
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of survey methodologies.

claim: The UK government is only providing £3 million/year (government and other sources) in targeted-funding for closing the award gap, equivalent to just £8 per BAME undergraduate/year.
source: Although the UK government has announced universities must remove the gap, it is only providing £3 million/year (government and other sources) in targeted-funding, equivalent to just £8 per BAME undergraduate/year (see Methods).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation of government funding (detailed in Methods).

claim: The UK government's commitment to funding for closing the award gap is only for 2–3 years.
source: In addition, the commitment is only for 2–3 years; yet the award gap will take several decades to close at current projection (AdvanceHE, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of government funding commitments.

claim: The award gap will take several decades to close at current projection.
source: In addition, the commitment is only for 2–3 years; yet the award gap will take several decades to close at current projection (AdvanceHE, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a report and inferred from the current rate of closure.

claim: Vanishing the award gap provides all employers with a major route to considerably close their ethnicity pay- and career-gaps and thus increases productivity through enhanced work-force diversity.
source: Vanishing the award gap should concern everyone. It provides all employers with a major route to considerably close their ethnicity pay- and career-gaps and thus increases productivity through enhanced work-force diversity.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the broader benefits of closing the award gap.

claim: Gap closure is the sole method available to universities to remove their breach of UK laws on race equality.
source: Furthermore, gap closure is the sole method available to universities to remove their breach of UK laws on race equality.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of UK equality law.

claim: The Dementia Discovery Fund is £250 million, an alliance of the UK government, global pharmaceutical companies, a UK charity, and global philanthropy which funds research into effective treatments for dementia, equivalent to £294 per UK patient.
source: This works elsewhere; take the Dementia Discovery Fund of £250 million, an alliance of the UK government, global pharmaceutical companies, a UK charity, and global philanthropy which funds research into effective treatments for dementia, equivalent to £294 per UK patient (see Methods).
evidence: The claim is based on data about the Dementia Discovery Fund (calculation detailed in Methods).

claim: Some pioneering initiatives in the UK and US have driven a two to four-fold increase in the proportion of PhD students from minority ethnic backgrounds in life sciences and physics over the last 3–6 years.
source: Some pioneering initiatives in the UK and US have driven a two to four-fold increase in the proportion of PhD students from minority ethnic backgrounds in life sciences and physics over the last 3–6 years (Hodapp and Woodle, 2017; Frank Bayliss, Tetrad Programme Office and Nadine Mogford personal communications).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and personal communications documenting successful initiatives.

claim: Where measured, retention of PhD students is higher than the national average in these schemes.
source: Where measured, retention of PhD students is also higher than the national average in these schemes (Hodapp and Woodle, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation documenting retention rates.

claim: The successful PhD programmes include the London (UK) Interdisciplinary Doctorate programme (LIDo), Tetrad PhD programme at UCSF, and the American Physical Society (APS) Bridge Programme.
source: These are the London (UK) Interdisciplinary Doctorate programme (LIDo), Tetrad PhD programme at UCSF, and the American Physical Society (APS) Bridge Programme (which has also increased female doctorates in physics).
evidence: The claim identifies specific successful programmes.

claim: $10 million from the US National Science Foundation has been awarded to extend the APS Bridge Programme to chemistry, geosciences, astronomy and material sciences.
source: $10 million from the US National Science Foundation has now been awarded to extend the APS Bridge Programme to chemistry, geosciences, astronomy and material sciences.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of NSF funding decisions.

claim: Research England and Office for Students have announced a joint funding call to support initiatives to increase access and participation for minority ethnic postgraduate research students.
source: In the UK, Research England and Office for Students have also recently announced a joint funding call to support initiatives to increase access and participation for minority ethnic postgraduate research students, initially planned for release in Autumn 2020 (but delayed due to COVID-19).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of UK funding announcements.

claim: Students consider the lack of ethnic diversity among senior leaders as the number one cause of the gap.
source: This may positively feedback on itself, as students consider the lack of ethnic diversity among senior leaders as the number one cause of the gap (Amos and Doku, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting student perspectives.

claim: In the UK, BAME (and also BME) is a nationally used term to represent all ethnic groups within Black, Asian, mixed ethnicity and other minority ethnic individuals (which includes white minority ethnic groups).
source: In the UK, BAME (and also BME) is a nationally used term to represent all ethnic groups within Black, Asian, mixed ethnicity and other minority ethnic individuals (which includes white minority ethnic groups).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of UK terminology.

claim: In the US, underrepresented minority (also known as URM) is more widely used and can refer to ethnicity or other qualifier; where 'underrepresented' indicates proportionally fewer than the proportion of that group in the population as a whole.
source: In the US, underrepresented minority (also known as URM) is instead more widely used and can refer to ethnicity or other qualifier; where 'underrepresented' indicates proportionally fewer than the proportion of that group in the population as a whole.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of US terminology.

claim: The US has a higher proportion of minority ethnic people (36% of the total population) compared to the UK's 14%.
source: The US has a higher proportion of minority ethnic people (36% of the total population) compared to the UK's 14%.
evidence: The claim is based on demographic data.

claim: Asian Americans, like white Americans, are overrepresented in PhD positions.
source: Also Asian Americans, like white Americans, are overrepresented in PhD positions (Hodapp and Woodle, 2017; NSF, 2019a), which is linked to these two groups scoring higher than all other ethnicities (and Asian higher than white) in graduate record exams (Miller and Stassun, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting PhD representation and exam scores.

claim: UCL classifies a student as having completed a module if a non-zero mark is awarded for the module overall.
source: UCL classifies a student as having completed a module if a non-zero mark is awarded for the module overall; and only these 'completed' students were included in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of UCL's classification system.

claim: A small minority of included students (4.5%: 36/792) completed the course (non-zero mark awarded), but UCL did not return a mark for either the exam (35 students), or exam and coursework (one student).
source: A small minority of included students (4.5%: 36/792) completed the course (non-zero mark awarded), but UCL did not return a mark for either the exam (35 students), or exam and coursework (one student).
evidence: The claim presents quantitative data about missing marks in the study cohort.

claim: Most recommendations on closing the award gap seemed based on informal observation (74.62%; 147/197).
source: Most recommendations seemed based on informal observation (74.62%; 147/197) and a few (4.57%; 9/197) could not be traced back to any obvious evidence.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of the evidence base for recommendations.

claim: A few recommendations (4.57%; 9/197) could not be traced back to any obvious evidence.
source: Most recommendations seemed based on informal observation (74.62%; 147/197) and a few (4.57%; 9/197) could not be traced back to any obvious evidence.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of the evidence base for recommendations.

claim: Ethnicity of respondents was not reported in 15/30 of surveys, interviews or discussions or other feedback included or cited in three major reports.
source: Ethnicity of respondents was not reported in 15/30 of surveys, interviews or discussions or other feedback included or cited in these three papers: ECU and HEA, 2008, Berry and Loke, 2011, Amos and Doku, 2019.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of survey methodologies.

claim: Out of the 15 surveys that did report ethnicity, 66.7% (10) only included responses from minority ethnic staff and students.
source: Out of the 15 that did report ethnicity, 66.7% (10) only included responses from minority ethnic staff and students.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's analysis of survey methodologies.

claim: UK Government Office for Students ('catalyst funding') and university (typically 'matched' funding) was identified from 'Addressing Barriers to Student Success Programme', which includes funds specifically aimed at reducing the award gap (10/17 projects).
source: UK Government Office for Students ('catalyst funding') and university (typically 'matched' funding) was identified from 'Addressing Barriers to Student Success Programme', which also includes funds that are specifically aimed at reducing the award gap (10/17 projects).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the funding programme.

claim: Total funding for the ten projects was £9,183,471 to be spent over typically three years (March 2017- October 2019).
source: Total funding for the ten projects was £9,183,471 to be spent over typically three years (March 2017- October 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the funding programme.

claim: The British Medical Council has awarded an additional £85,000 to individual researchers for award gap research.
source: The British Medical Council has awarded an additional £85,000 to individual researchers.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of BMC funding.

claim: There are 360,650 UK-domiciled, BAME undergraduate students in the UK.
source: There are 360,650 UK-domiciled, BAME undergraduate students in the UK (Higher Education Statistics Agency).
evidence: The claim is based on data from HESA.

claim: UK government and other funding for closing the award gap is £8.49 per BAME student per year.
source: Thus, UK government and other funding is £8.49 per BAME student per year (and the funding has now ended).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from funding and student numbers.

claim: There are about 850,000 dementia patients in the UK (as of 2021).
source: The Dementia Discovery Fund is £250 million and there are about 850,000 dementia patients in the UK (as of 2021) giving £294 funding per patient.
evidence: The claim is based on data about dementia prevalence.

claim: This study predates the COVID-19 pandemic and all data are of original assessments and degree classifications as they stood prior to universities changing them in March 2020 as a result of the pandemic.
source: This study predates the COVID-19 pandemic and all data (including all citations) are of original assessments and degree classifications as they stood prior to universities changing them in March 2020 as a result of the pandemic.
evidence: The claim clarifies the temporal context of the data collection.
